The client asked why her adviser's high conviction pick is only 5% of the portfolio: risk limits.
terms.fill: The PM gave the stock a 7% weight, three times the usual, because it was her ____ idea.
wrong: A trade the compliance team has approved
A position held for many years
A view shared by most of the street

terms.short: Possible loss set against possible gain
terms.definition: The possible loss on a trade set against the possible gain, often as a ratio. Buying at 1,000 with a stop at 960 and a target at 1,120 risks 40 to make 120, a 1:3 risk-reward.
examples: The risk-reward isn't there: we're risking 8% to make 5%.
At these levels the risk-reward favours selling the rally.
The client asked whether to buy now; the analyst said the risk-reward is poor after the rally.
terms.fill: With a stop 50 points below and a target 150 above, the trade offers a 1:3 ____.
wrong: Return earned per unit of volatility
Share of trades that end in profit
Extra return paid for taking on risk

calcs.q: You buy at ₹500 with a stop-loss at ₹480 and a target of ₹560. What is the risk-reward?

tf.s: A good risk-reward ratio on its own makes a trade worth taking.
tf.why: It also depends on how likely each outcome is. A 1:3 trade that hits its stop 90% of the time loses money.

aliases: is it a hedge or a view?
terms.short: Is it cutting risk or adding a bet?
terms.definition: A PM's question about a new position: does it reduce a risk the book already has, or does it express a fresh opinion? A 'hedge' that only pays if a forecast comes true is really a view, and is sized and judged like one.
examples: You bought Bank Nifty puts against your bank longs, fine. But three times the exposure? Is it a hedge or a view?
Call it what it is: shorting IT stocks when the book owns no IT stocks is a view, not a hedge.
Risk asked the PM whether the big index short is a hedge or a view.
terms.fill: Buying puts worth three times the book's exposure doesn't just cut risk, so the PM asked whether it was ____.
wrong: Should the hedge be short- or long-dated?
Is the trade in cash or in F&O?
Is the order passive or aggressive?

terms.short: Cut longs and shorts together
terms.definition: To shrink a long-short book's gross exposure by cutting both the longs and the shorts, so the net stays about the same. Funds de-gross when volatility or crowding rises.
examples: Crowded shorts are squeezing; let's de-gross by a third and keep the net flat.
Prime brokers saw funds de-gross across the board last week.
Risk told the fund to de-gross by a quarter when the shorts started squeezing.
terms.fill: The fund cut both its longs and its shorts by a third and kept its net exposure the same: it chose to ____.
wrong: Sell only the longs to go net short
Add to both longs and shorts
Swap gross returns for net returns

calcs.q: A fund is ₹500 crore long and ₹300 crore short. It de-grosses by cutting both sides by 20%. What is its new gross exposure?
calcs.why: Longs fall to ₹400 crore and shorts to ₹240 crore. Gross is 400 + 240 = ₹640 crore; net falls from ₹200 crore to ₹160 crore.

terms.short: Move longs and shorts closer to balance
terms.definition: To reduce a book's net exposure, the gap between its longs and shorts, so it depends less on the market's direction. You can sell longs, add shorts or sell index futures.
examples: We're 40% net long into the Fed meeting. Bring the net down to 15% with Nifty futures.
If you don't want to sell your best longs, bring the net down with an index short.
The PM decided to bring the net down before the election by selling index futures.
terms.fill: Worried about a fall, the PM sold Nifty futures so the book went from 50% net long to 20%: she chose to ____.
wrong: Lower the fund's fees after costs
Cut longs and shorts by the same share
Reduce the profit after tax

terms.short: Same money on the long and short sides
terms.definition: A long-short book with the same value of longs as of shorts, so its net exposure is zero. It can still move with the market if the longs have a higher beta than the shorts.
examples: We're dollar-neutral, ₹100 crore each side, but the longs are high-beta mid caps, so we're still long the market.
A rupee-neutral pair: ₹50 lakh long ICICI Bank against ₹50 lakh short HDFC Bank.
The client asked whether her dollar-neutral fund can still lose on a market fall: yes, if its longs are riskier.
terms.fill: With ₹200 crore of longs and ₹200 crore of shorts, the book is ____, though not necessarily beta-neutral.
wrong: Holding only US dollar assets
Hedged against moves in the rupee
Same number of shares long and short

tf.s: A dollar-neutral book can still lose money when the whole market falls.
tf.why: If the longs have a higher beta than the shorts, the book is still long the market.

terms.short: Long and short betas cancel out
terms.definition: A book whose beta-weighted longs and shorts cancel, so small market moves leave it roughly flat. A book of high-beta longs and low-beta shorts needs more rupees of shorts than of longs to get there.
examples: Longs have a beta of 1.3 and shorts 0.9, so ₹100 crore long needs about ₹144 crore short to be beta-neutral.
We run beta-neutral, so the Nifty's 3% fall barely showed up in the PnL.
Risk rebalances the hedges daily to keep the book beta-neutral.
terms.fill: ₹100 crore of longs with a beta of 1.2 against ₹120 crore of shorts with a beta of 1.0 leaves the book ____.
wrong: Same money on the long and short sides
Holding only stocks with zero beta
A book with no stock-specific risk

calcs.q: Your longs are ₹50 crore with a beta of 1.4. Your shorts have a beta of 0.7. How much do you need short to be beta-neutral?
calcs.why: Long beta exposure is 50 × 1.4 = ₹70 crore. Shorts with a beta of 0.7 need 70 ÷ 0.7 = ₹100 crore.

terms.short: Risk a PM or strategy is allowed to run
terms.definition: The amount of risk, measured as volatility, VaR or a drawdown limit, given to a strategy or a PM. Capital follows from it: a calm strategy gets more capital than a volatile one for the same risk budget.
examples: Your risk budget is 3% annual vol of the fund; you're using 2.4%.
We gave the stat-arb book a bigger risk budget after two good years.
The PM asked for a bigger risk budget after the signal's strong year.
terms.fill: Each PM gets a ____ of ₹5 crore of daily VaR and can't exceed it without approval.
wrong: Money set aside for the risk team's pay
Total margin blocked at the broker
Fees charged for risk reports

terms.short: Fall from the peak that triggers a cut
terms.definition: How far a PM or strategy may fall from its peak before risk is cut. A common setup: lose 5% from the high and your size is halved; lose 10% and you stop trading.
examples: You're 6% off the peak against an 8% drawdown budget, so the next 2% decides your year.
Our drawdown budget is 10%; at 5% the size is halved automatically.
The client asked why the fund cut its bets after a 6% fall: it had used half its drawdown budget.
terms.fill: The fund's rule is to halve a PM's capital once she is 5% below her peak: a ____.
wrong: Money kept aside to repay loans
Share of profit paid as a bonus
Limit on how much margin can be used

tf.s: Near the limit of a drawdown budget, the usual rule is to cut position sizes, not raise them.
tf.why: Swinging harder to win the loss back is how a small drawdown becomes a blow-up.

terms.short: Smaller positions in more volatile names
terms.definition: Setting each position's size so it carries the same risk: divide a fixed risk amount by the asset's volatility. A stock that moves 3% a day gets a third of the rupees of one that moves 1%.
examples: Size by vol: ₹1 crore in the bank that moves 1% a day, ₹33 lakh in the small cap that moves 3%.
Equal rupees in every name means your small caps carry all the risk; size by vol.
Risk tells new PMs to size by vol, so no single stock dominates the book's risk.
terms.fill: Giving a stock that swings 2% a day half the rupees of one that swings 1% is how you ____.
wrong: Buy more when the market is volatile
Put equal money in every stock
Size trades by their trading volume

calcs.q: You want each position to risk ₹2 lakh on a typical day. A stock moves about 1.6% a day. How big should the position be?

terms.short: Days needed to exit without moving price
terms.definition: How many days it would take to sell a position while trading only a set share of daily volume, often 10% to 20%. Risk teams cap it, because a big position in a thin stock can't be cut quickly in a crisis.
examples: At 20% participation that's 6 days to liquidate, and the limit is 3.
The small-cap long is fine on VaR, but it's 15 days to liquidate. That's the real risk.
Risk caps each position at three days to liquidate at 20% of daily volume.
terms.fill: Holding 30 lakh shares of a stock that trades 10 lakh a day, at 20% of volume, works out at 15 ____.
wrong: Days left until the contract expires
Time for a trade to settle at the depository
Days a broker waits before a margin call

calcs.q: You hold 12 lakh shares. The stock trades 20 lakh shares a day and you'll take at most 15% of volume. How many days to liquidate?
calcs.why: 15% of 20 lakh is 3 lakh shares a day. 12 lakh ÷ 3 lakh = 4 days.

terms.short: How much you lose if you're wrong
terms.definition: The possible loss on a trade or a stock if things go badly. 'What's the downside?' asks for a number: where it trades if the idea fails, and how much the book loses.
examples: Upside is 20% to our target; downside is 10% if the results disappoint.
What's the downside if the RBI doesn't cut? About ₹40 lakh at the current size.
The client asked what the downside is if the market falls 20%: about ₹4 lakh on her portfolio.
terms.fill: If the deal falls through, the stock goes back to ₹800 from ₹1,000, so the ____ is 20%.
wrong: Possible rise from here
Lowest price of the day
Fall already seen this year

terms.short: Past an agreed risk or loss limit
terms.definition: When a position, exposure or loss goes past a limit the risk team has set. A breach is logged and escalated, and the trader usually has to cut back by a deadline or get approval to stay over.
examples: You're at 112% of your gross limit. That's a breach; get it back under by the close.
A soft breach sends an email; a hard breach means the risk team cuts the position for you.
Risk logs every limit breach and the time it took to fix.
terms.fill: Her loss hit ₹1.2 crore against a ₹1 crore daily limit, so the risk team logged a ____ and froze new trades.
wrong: A break in the trading system
A trade that crosses the spread
A price move through support

terms.short: Most you may hold in one name or contract
terms.definition: A cap on how big a position can be, in rupees, shares, contracts or share of volume. Firms set their own for risk; exchanges and SEBI also set limits in F&O, such as each stock's market-wide position limit.
examples: The single-name limit is 5% of the book, so the most I can own is ₹25 crore.
We can't add more futures; we're at the client-level position limit.
The client asked why her broker wouldn't let her add more futures: she'd hit the exchange's position limit.
terms.fill: No stock may be more than 5% of the fund: that's the fund's ____ on single names.
wrong: Price at which a stop-loss order fires
Margin a broker blocks per lot
Largest order the exchange takes at once

terms.short: Too much riding on a few names or bets
terms.definition: The risk of having a large share of the book in a few stocks, one sector or one theme. Measures like VaR can understate it, because one bad event hits a big piece of the book at once.
examples: The top five names are 45% of the book; that's concentration risk whatever the VaR says.
Three of your 'different' longs are all PSU banks. That's concentration.
The client asked why the adviser worries about her portfolio: 60% in one stock is concentration risk.
terms.fill: With 60% of the book in three bank stocks, the risk report flagged ____.
wrong: Risk of losing focus on a long day
Risk from trading too many stocks
Risk that a fund's units are all sold at once

terms.short: What the book loses in a set bad scenario
terms.definition: The loss the book would take in a defined extreme scenario, such as the Nifty falling 10% in a day, a repeat of March 2020, or volatility doubling. Limits are often set on stress loss as well as VaR, since VaR ignores the worst days.
examples: Stress loss on a 15% gap down is ₹18 crore against a limit of ₹20 crore.
VaR looks small because the book is short options, but the stress loss on a vol spike is huge.
The board asked for the stress loss on a 2008-style crash before approving the new fund.
terms.fill: If the Nifty fell 10% overnight and India VIX doubled, the book would lose ₹8 crore: that's its ____ in that scenario.
wrong: Average daily loss over the last year
Loss a trader can take before a review
Loss caused by stressed staff making errors

tf.s: A short option book can show a small VaR and a large stress loss.
tf.why: VaR is built from normal days. Selling options earns small amounts until a big move, which only a stress scenario captures.

terms.short: Day's loss at which trading stops
terms.definition: The most a trader, desk or strategy may lose in one day. Hit it and positions are cut or new trading stops for the day. Many intraday traders set one for themselves too.
examples: My daily loss limit is ₹2 lakh; I'm at ₹1.6 lakh, so I'm only closing trades now.
The algo hit its daily loss limit at 11:40 and switched itself off.
The client's daily loss limit on her app stops her trading once she's down ₹5,000.
terms.fill: After losing ₹50,000 by noon, his ____, he closed everything and stopped for the day.
wrong: Most a stock can fall in one day
Daily margin the broker blocks
Loss carried over to the next day

terms.short: One step that cancels orders and halts trading
terms.definition: A control that, in one action, cancels all open orders and blocks new ones, for an algo, a desk or a whole account. Firms use it when an algo misbehaves; many Indian brokers also let retail traders use one to stop themselves trading for a while.
examples: The algo started sending orders in a loop, so we hit the kill switch.
After three losing days he used his broker's kill switch to block F&O trading for a week.
The client asked whether her broker has a kill switch to stop her trading after a bad day: yes, in the app.
terms.fill: When the strategy began firing duplicate orders, the desk used the ____ to cancel everything and block new orders.
wrong: Exchange-wide halt after a 10% fall
Order that closes a position at a set price
Rule that stops a stock trading for a day

tf.s: A market-wide circuit breaker and a firm's kill switch are the same thing.
tf.why: The exchange's circuit breaker halts the whole market; a kill switch is a firm's or trader's own control over its orders.

terms.short: The move that hurts the most people
terms.definition: The market move that would hurt the most investors, given how they are positioned. If nearly everyone is short or underweight, the pain trade is a sharp rally. Desks watch it because crowded positions unwind violently.
examples: FIIs are heavily short index futures, so the pain trade is higher.
Everyone's hiding in defensives; the pain trade is a jump in the beaten-down cyclicals.
The strategist says the pain trade is a rally, since most funds are holding cash.
terms.fill: Funds were heavily underweight Indian banks, so a sharp bank rally was the ____ that forced them to chase.
wrong: A trade that loses money slowly
A trade done only to cut tax
A trade kept open out of stubbornness

terms.short: Risk of rare, very large losses
terms.definition: The risk of rare, extreme moves far out in the tails of the return distribution, such as a 10% one-day fall. Market returns have fat tails, so these happen more often than a normal distribution predicts.
examples: Selling far OTM puts makes money most months, but the tail risk can take a year's profit in a day.
We buy cheap puts every month as a tail-risk hedge.
The client asked why her fund buys cheap puts every month: to cover tail risk.
terms.fill: Short option books earn steady premium but carry ____: a rare crash can wipe out years of gains.
wrong: Risk in the last hour of trading
Risk that a trend runs on too long
Risk from copying other traders

tf.s: Five-standard-deviation daily falls happen far more often in real markets than a normal distribution predicts.

terms.short: In a crash, everything falls together
terms.definition: The tendency of assets that usually move separately to fall together in a panic, as investors sell whatever they can. Diversification that works in calm markets can vanish just when it's needed.
examples: Our 30 longs looked diversified until March 2020, when correlations went to one.
Don't count on diversification in a crisis; correlations go to one.
Risk plans for the day when correlations go to one, so diversification can't be counted on.
terms.fill: In the panic, stocks, credit and even gold fell on the same days, as ____.
wrong: Two stocks become one after a merger
Every trade ends up at the same price
A hedge ratio is set to exactly one

terms.short: Who trades against you, and why?
terms.definition: A question to ask of any trade or edge: who is taking the opposite position, and why are they willing to? If you can't name them, you may be the one with less information.
examples: Who's on the other side? If it's a fund rebalancing, great. If it's someone with better information, we're the mug.
Before you buy that block, ask who's on the other side and why they're selling in size.
The client asked how to judge a hot tip; the adviser's first question was who's on the other side?
terms.fill: Before trusting a strategy's edge, ask ____: a forced seller, or someone who knows more than you?
wrong: Who will clear the trade for you?
Which exchange will show the trade?
Who books the trade in the back office?

terms.short: Close positions before a big announcement
terms.definition: To close or hedge positions before a known event like results, an RBI policy, the Budget or an election count, so a surprise can't hurt. It gives up any gain from the event in return for no gap risk.
examples: I'm flat into the policy; the setup isn't worth the gap risk.
We go flat into results on single names and only re-enter after the earnings call.
The PM stayed flat into the event, so the surprise policy cost her nothing.
terms.fill: Not wanting to guess the RBI's decision, the trader closed all her rate trades the day before: she went ____.
wrong: Buy before a known event to profit
Keep positions the same size all week
Trade only when prices are flat

terms.short: Risk the price jumps past your stop
terms.definition: The risk that a price opens far from the last close, skipping past a stop-loss. Overnight news, results or global moves can gap a stock 10%, so a stop at −2% fills much worse.
examples: Your stop is at 2%, but on results day the gap risk is 8%.
Holding short options over a weekend carries gap risk that intraday stops can't cover.
The client asked why her stop-loss didn't save her: gap risk, as the stock opened 15% lower.
terms.fill: The stock closed at ₹1,000 and opened at ₹900 after bad results, so the stop at ₹980 filled near ₹900: that's ____.
wrong: Gap between the bid and the offer
Risk of a gap in the price data
Gap between the futures and spot prices

tf.s: A stop-loss order guarantees your exit price even if the stock gaps down overnight.
tf.why: The stop fires at the open, at whatever price is there, which can be far below the stop.

terms.short: Cash or risk kept back for later
terms.definition: Cash or unused risk budget held back so you can act when a better chance comes, such as after a sell-off. Keeping dry powder costs some return in quiet markets.
examples: We're 80% invested and keeping dry powder for the IPO pipeline.
Don't use the whole risk budget in January; keep some dry powder.
The client asked why her fund holds 10% cash: it's dry powder for buying in a fall.
terms.fill: The fund kept 15% in cash as ____ to buy if the market fell after the election.
wrong: Money lost to fees and costs
Gains not yet taxed
Cash a broker holds as margin
